new_statements.quote: Avikam has two contrastive lexical tones, High and Low. It has also a downstepped High tone. There are no contrastive lexical Mid tones. The language has no contrastive contour tones on monosyllables, though it has, according to Herault (1982:267), High-Low and Low-High contours on some syllables in initial, medial and final positions. In verbs, contour tones are clearly derived tones.
new_statements.citation: Ahoua, Firmin. 2009. The Phonology-Syntax Interface in Avikam. Legon Journal of the Humanities 20: 123-149.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Avikam is a two-tone language (H, L, plus downstepped H) with lexical tonal minimal pairs; the article's prosodic constituents (tonal foot, prosodic word, phonological phrase) are defined by a Tone Lowering rule, and no word stress or accent is mentioned at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; the tonal statement notes downstep position is unpredictable and surface contours (HL, LH) occur on some syllables per Hérault 1982:267.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical word (citation forms carry a prefix vowel; CV roots do not occur in isolation); the article is about tone across words and phrases in the Kpanda dialect of Grand Lahou.
new_statements.identity_note: Ahoua 2009 describes the Kpanda dialect of Avikam (Grand Lahou coast, fieldwork 1999); he notes at least two dialects differing only in minor segmental correspondences. Same language-level glottocode avik1243; no separate dialect glottocode found.

sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent anywhere in the 27 pages (grep for stress/accent/prominence: no hits). Sec. 4.2 p. 128: two contrastive lexical tones H and L plus downstepped H, no lexical Mid, no contrastive contours on monosyllables; the paper treats prosodic domains (tonal foot, prosodic word, phonological phrase) purely in terms of a Tone Lowering rule. Kpanda dialect, fieldwork 1999.
